description_full: Exelixis, Inc., an oncology company, focuses on the discovery, development, and commercialization of new medicines for difficult-to-treat cancers in the United States. The company offers CABOMETYX tablets for the treatment of patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma who received prior anti-angiogenic therapy; and COMETRIQ capsules for the treatment of progressive and metastatic medullary thyroid cancer. Its CABOMETYX and COMETRIQ are derived from cabozantinib, an inhibitor of multiple tyrosine kinases, including MET, AXL, RET, and VEGF receptors. The company also offers COTELLIC, an inhibitor of MEK as a combination regimen to treat specific forms of advanced melanoma; and MINNEBRO, an oral non-steroidal selective blocker of the mineralocorticoid receptor for the treatment of hypertension in Japan. It develops zanzalintinib, a novel, potent oral inhibitor of kinases, including the TAM kinases, MET, and VEGF receptors; XL309, a small molecule inhibitor of USP1, a synthetic lethal target in the context of BRCA-mutated tumors; XB010, an antibody-drug conjugates (ADC) consisting of a MMAE payload conjugated to a monoclonal antibody targeting the tumor antigen 5T4; XB628, a first-in-class bispecific antibody that targets programmed cell death ligand 1and natural killer cell receptor group 2A; and XB371, a next-generation tissue factor targeting ADC with a topoisomerase inhibitor payload. It has research collaborations and license agreements with Ipsen Pharma SAS; Takeda Pharmaceutical Company Ltd.; F. Hoffmann-La Roche Ltd.; Catalent, Inc.; Iconic Therapeutics, Inc.; Adagene Inc.; Invenra, Inc.; Genentech, Inc.; Bristol-Myers Squibb Company; and Daiichi Sankyo Company, Limited, as well as business development activities and other collaborations. The company was formerly known as Exelixis Pharmaceuticals, Inc. and changed its name to Exelixis, Inc. in February 2000. Exelixis, Inc. was incorporated in 1994 and is headquartered in Alameda, California.

financial_summary: Exelixis, Inc. is a large-cap healthcare business with a $16.8B market cap on $2.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years and +51% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 32% against a 9% cost of capital — a 23-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $876M in free cash flow — roughly 38 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.13× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 4.3× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 462 companies in the universe; the top four hold 35% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 41% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 6% below the high.

val: The stock trades only 14% below its DCF fair value of $80.19, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 42%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $60.75 to $110 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 26% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.3% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 32% clears the cost of capital of 8.7% by 23pp, the mark of a value creator.
It converts 38% of revenue into free cash flow, or 33% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.13x.

hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $896.9M.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 12.9% over 3 years, 18.6% over 5 years and 51.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 114%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 37.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.99, a backlog worth 5% of annual revenue, deferred revenue up 18% and 22 active clinical trials.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (0.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 52, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.

Insiders have only sold over the past year (9 sales, net $10.8M sold).
It returns 5.6% a year to shareholders (5.6% in buybacks).
